excerpt_original: Tate Britain is devoting a major exhibition to the 1990s, bringing together photographers Juergen Teller, Corinne Day, Nick Knight and Wolfgang Tillmans alongside artists Damien Hirst and Sarah Lucas and designer Alexander McQueen. A decade in which art, fashion and the street…

blocks.text: Some decades look like laboratory accidents: you mix the wrong chemicals, something explodes, and the result gets retroactively labeled a cultural revolution. Britain in the 1990s was one of them. Named fashion director of i-D magazine in 1991 at eighteen, Edward Enninful turned it into the organ of London’s counterculture, amplifying urban voices and avant-gardes alike, before taking the helm of British Vogue for seven years.

He now serves as curator of this retrospective. “Magazines weren’t just documenting culture,” he writes in Tate Etc. , the museum’s own journal, “they were helping to create it.” London at the end of that century bore this out: the magazines were the crucible where everything fused, populated by the same artists, shaped by the same squats, the same freezing studios, the same overheated clubs.

In the pages of The Face, Corinne Day, Juergen Teller and their peers established themselves, in the Tate’s words, “at the forefront of defining a new anti-fashion grunge style.” A pioneer of heroin chic, Corinne Day introduced Kate Moss at fifteen, with a documentary intimacy that dismantled the manufactured glamour of previous decades. Juergen Teller, for his part, gave us Young Pink Kate (1998), the young model caught in the raw light of a disposable flash, as if just woken, irreverent and magnetic.

blocks.text: Nick Knight photographed dancer David Toole, who had his legs amputated in early childhood, for the “Fashion-Able” issue of Dazed & Confused , guest-edited by Alexander McQueen to showcase models with disabilities: a landmark in the history of inclusion. Wolfgang Tillmans closes the chapter with “Concorde Grid” (1997), a series of snapshots of Concorde in flight over London, shot through with “the dual feelings of optimism and anxiety induced by the impending millennium.”

The Young British Artists, meanwhile, had not waited for the millennium to settle their scores. Tracey Emin, Sam Taylor-Johnson and Sarah Lucas “captivated the public with their anarchic spirit and frank work tackling agency, identity and class.” For his zoological vitrines, Damien Hirst submerged dead animals, whole or bisected (sharks, cows, lambs) in formaldehyde-filled tanks, “removing the artist’s hand altogether, the antithesis to low-fi grunge”: death as ready-made. In Chicken Knickers , Sarah Lucas posed a raw plucked chicken against a nude figure wearing a pair of granny underwear, elevating vulgarity into critical weapon while reducing the female body to its crudest terms.

Fashion completes the picture, though to reduce it to that role would be to miss the point. Alexander McQueen, John Galliano and Vivienne Westwood staged shows that were “provocative, dramatic and sometimes nightmarish,” belonging as much, if not more, to performance art as to couture. Hussein Chalayan conceived “design-led clothing inspired by everyday objects,” where exile and identity were literally worn on the body. Ozwald Boateng cut Savile Row to the measure of his Ghanaian heritage, while Mark Leckey, with his video Fiorucci Made Me Hardcore (1999), distilled the quiet melancholy of club nights into art: gestures, all of them refusing any hierarchy between disciplines.

blocks.text: What Tate Britain achieves here carries a gentle irony: opening its doors to a scene that defined itself by its contempt for institutions. By hanging these works beneath its neoclassical ceilings, the museum confers on them a legitimacy they never sought, and might well have disowned. Here they are, canonized against their will.
“The 90s: Art and Fashion” is on view at Tate Britain , London, from October 8, 2026 to February 14, 2027.
